narrative:
The model estimated a 74.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, that is roughly a three-in-four risk, and the law school treated that as too high to admit you.

The denial was driven most strongly by your third-year class-position decile, which was 1.00, compared with an average of about 5.79 among accepted students. That was the single largest factor and it pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year decile, also 1.00 and far from the accepted average of 6.00, was the second-largest factor and likewise increased the predicted risk. The third most influential factor was your part-time status. Most accepted students in this group were full-time—about 92.8%—while only 7.2% were part-time; your part-time plan therefore added to the concern that you might not pass.

Although other details such as your LSAT score of 31 and undergraduate GPA of 2.70 are below the accepted averages, the strongest explanation for the rejection is the combination of your class-position deciles and part-time enrollment. To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic standing, consider enrolling full-time or reducing work hours during law study, and build a concrete bar-exam preparation plan. You should also ask admissions for feedback and, if you reapply, provide evidence of academic improvement and a realistic schedule for full-time study.
